extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators, appellate advocates, and federal judges
extracted.subtask_description: Legal standards and precedent governing when a prior PTAB final written decision (IPR) can preclude assertion of patent claims in district court, including the effect of differing burdens of proof and claim similarity analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collateral estoppel elements (Third Circuit)
rubrics_metrics.description: "(1) the identical issue was previously adjudicated; (2) the issue was actually litigated; (3) the previous determination was necessary to the decision; and (4) the party being precluded from relitigating the issue was fully represented in the prior action." (Jean Alexander Cosmetics, Inc. v. L’Oreal USA, Inc.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: District court applied these four requirements as the starting point for estoppel analysis; the opinion notes the parties did not dispute that the second and fourth elements were met in this case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exception where second action applies a different legal standard (burden of proof)
rubrics_metrics.description: Collateral estoppel is "subject to certain well-known exceptions," including when "the second action involves application of a different legal standard," such as a different burden of proof. (B & B Hardware, Inc. v. Hargis Indus., Inc.; Grogan v. Garner)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the prior proceeding used a lower standard (e.g., preponderance) and the later proceeding requires a higher standard (e.g., clear and convincing), preclusion generally should not apply; see also Wright & Miller on the rule that preclusion under a lower standard is not entitled in a later action requiring a higher standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of a final written Board decision on the same claim (XY rule / cancellation doctrine)
rubrics_metrics.description: Once this court affirms the Board’s decision that a patent claim is unpatentable, the same claim cannot be asserted in district court because the claim has been finally held unpatentable and subjected to "retroactive cancellation." (XY, LLC v. Trans Ova Genetics; explanation in ParkerVision)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The preclusive effect in this situation is grounded not on the Board’s fact findings but on the legal consequence that the claim no longer exists following final cancellation/affirmance; this is distinct from using Board fact-findings to estop different claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: IPR-to-district collateral estoppel is barred when relying on Board fact-findings proved under a lower burden
rubrics_metrics.description: A prior final written decision of the Board of unpatentability on separate patent claims reached under a preponderance of the evidence standard cannot collaterally estop a patentee from asserting other, unadjudicated patent claims in district court litigation where invalidity must be proved by clear and convincing evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Court holds dismissal was inappropriate because applying estoppel here would deprive patent owners of property rights without the statutorily-prescribed clear and convincing proof required in district court (citing ParkerVision and Microsoft v. i4i).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ohio Willow Wood rule on immaterial differences between claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Collateral estoppel may apply to patent claims that were not previously adjudicated if the differences between the unadjudicated claims and the adjudicated claims "do not materially alter the question of invalidity." (Ohio Willow Wood Co. v. Alps S., LLC)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ohio Willow Wood addresses district-court-to-district-court preclusion where the burden/standard is the same; the Federal Circuit here explains that Ohio Willow Wood does not resolve Board-to-district preclusion where the burdens differ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards of review and pleading standard
rubrics_metrics.description: A district court’s dismissal for failure to state a claim is reviewed de novo under the regional circuit law; the Third Circuit reviews such dismissals de novo. Collateral estoppel application is also reviewed de novo under the regional circuit law when it implicates substantive patent-law issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For motions to dismiss, the complaint must "contain sufficient factual matter, accepted as true, to state a claim to relief that is plausible on its face." (Ashcroft v. Iqbal). Cite Content Extraction & Transmission LLC v. Wells Fargo Bank for standard-of-review precedent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof distinction: IPR (preponderance) vs district court (clear and convincing)
rubrics_metrics.description: In IPR, the petitioner must prove unpatentability by a preponderance of the evidence; in district court, invalidity must be proven by clear and convincing evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the burdens differ, prior fact findings in an IPR (preponderance) generally cannot be given collateral estoppel effect in district court (clear and convincing) absent the special circumstance where the same claim has been finally canceled/affirmed; see Grogan, B & B Hardware, ParkerVision, and Microsoft v. i4i.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption of validity for unadjudicated claims
rubrics_metrics.description: "Those claims remain presumptively valid" until they have been found unpatentable and finally cancelled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The opinion emphasizes that unadjudicated claims continue to exist and carry the presumption of validity; collateral estoppel cannot be used to strip that presumption by importing lower-burden fact findings from IPRs.
